title: Comparison of the Safety and Efficacy of Remimazolam for Sedation in Adults Undergoing Fiberoptic Bronchoscopy: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
authors: Lee S, Na HS, Koo BW, Joo DH, Shin HJ
abstract: BACKGROUND: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy requires effective sedation to ensure patient comfort while preserving gas exchange, hemodynamic stability, and predictable recovery. Remimazolam, a novel ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine, has emerged as a potential alternative to traditional sedatives. However, its safety and efficacy compared with those of other sedatives remain under investigation. This meta-analysis evaluated the safety and efficacy of remimazolam versus dexmedetomidine, midazolam, and propofol in adults undergoing fiberoptic bronchoscopy. METHODS: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted using 5 databases through January 2026. Outcomes included respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia, time to target sedation depth, procedure success rate, emergence time, and postanesthesia care unit (PACU) stay. Relative risks (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% CI were calculated using a random-effects model. RESULTS: Sixteen RCTs (2325 patients) were included. Remimazolam significantly reduced respiratory depression (RR: 0.51, 95% CI: 0.36-0.73, P<0.001), hypotension (RR: 0.50, 95% CI: 0.34-0.73, P<0.001), and bradycardia (RR: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.22-0.65, P=0.001) versus controls. Sedation onset was faster than dexmedetomidine (MD: -2.19 min), but slower than propofol (MD: 0.49 min). Success rates were comparable across groups (RR: 1.12, 95% CI: 0.98-1.28, P=0.097). Compared with dexmedetomidine and midazolam, remimazolam shortened emergence (MD: -1.79 and -4.37 min, respectively) and PACU stay (MD: -3.58 and -6.70 min). CONCLUSION: Remimazolam provides effective sedation for fiberoptic bronchoscopy with advantages in terms of respiratory and hemodynamic safety, rapid recovery, and procedural efficiency.

title: Prediction Models for Delayed Bleeding After Colorectal Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection: A Systematic Review and Critical Appraisal.
authors: Miao D, Hou Z, Ge Y, Qi H
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although many predictive models have been developed or validated for delayed bleeding after colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), their methodological quality and clinical utility remain uncertain. We systematically reviewed and critically appraised all available predictive models for this outcome. METHODS: We searched five databases through March 2026 for observational studies that developed or validated prediction models or scoring systems for delayed bleeding after colorectal ESD in adults (≥18 years). Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using PROBAST. RESULTS: Of 25,177 records screened, five studies reporting five predictive models were included. The incidence of delayed bleeding ranged from 2.9% to 9.9%. The most commonly used predictors were lesion location and lesion size. Discrimination in derivation cohorts ranged from 0.726 to 0.890, internal validation areas under the curve [AUCs] ranged from 0.739 to 0.870, and the externally validated model achieved an AUC of 0.634. All studies were judged to have a high risk of bias, mainly because of inadequate reporting in the predictor, outcome, and analysis domains, although most had low concerns regarding applicability. CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review identified five predictive models for delayed bleeding after colorectal ESD. Lesion location and size were the most frequently reported predictors. Discriminative performance varied across derivation and validation cohorts, with suboptimal external-validation results. All models had a high risk of bias per PROBAST (low concerns regarding applicability); therefore, their findings should be interpreted cautiously.

title: No superiority of double drains over single drainage after tissue expander-based breast reconstruction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Delgado LM, Kodalak EA, Machado GF, Sreepathi D, Amaral RXA, Poggi AC, de Sena GBX, Santos LRA
abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal number of drains after postmastectomy tissue expander (TE)-based breast reconstruction remains uncertain. Although double-drain placement may theoretically improve fluid clearance and reduce seroma formation, it may also increase patient discomfort, prolong drain-related morbidity, and potentially increase contamination risk. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared postoperative outcomes between single- and double-drain strategies following TE-based breast reconstruction. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 16, 2026. Comparative studies evaluating single versus double drains after postmastectomy TE-based reconstruction were included. Outcomes of interest included seroma formation, surgical site infection (SSI), hematoma, return to the operating room, skin flap necrosis, drain duration, and TE/implant-related complications. Risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I and certainty of evidence with the GRADE approach. RESULTS: Three retrospective observational studies comprising 1350 reconstructions were included, with 660 reconstructions in the single-drain group and 690 in the double-drain group. There were no significant differences between single- and double-drain strategies in seroma formation (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.49; p = 0.54; I² = 63%), SSI (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.37; p = 0.93; I² = 39%), hematoma (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.63; p = 0.61; I² = 0%), return to the operating room (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.43; p = 0.29; I² = 12%), skin flap necrosis (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.19; p = 0.22; I² = 0%), or drain duration (MD -3.90 days, 95% CI -12.42 to 4.63; p = 0.37; I² = 97%). Leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter the findings for seroma formation or SSI. Certainty of evidence was low for seroma, SSI, and skin flap necrosis, and very low for hematoma, return to the operating room, and drain duration. CONCLUSION: Current evidence does not demonstrate a benefit of routine double-drain placement after TE-based breast reconstruction. The certainty of evidence was low, and these findings indicate a lack of demonstrated benefit rather than equivalence between the two strategies. Selective second-drain placement based on intraoperative findings remains reasonable, and adequately powered prospective studies are needed.

title: Endobronchial Valves for Persistent Air Leak and Bronchopleural Fistula in Children: A Systematic Review of Indications, Procedural Approaches, and Outcomes.
authors: Mahindrakar N, Bhandari P, Yedatore R, Vorakunthada Y, Lilitwat W
abstract: BACKGROUND: Persistent air leak (PAL) and bronchopleural fistula (BPF) are uncommon but important complications in children, particularly with necrotizing pneumonia, postoperative injury, malignancy, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). When conservative therapy fails or surgery is high-risk, endobronchial or intrabronchial valve placement has emerged as a minimally invasive bronchoscopic option. This systematic review summarizes the published pediatric experience, focusing on indications, procedural approach, and outcomes. METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to June 2026, with Google Scholar and reference lists screened; no language limits applied. Eligible studies reported pediatric or late-adolescent patients who underwent bronchoscopic valve placement for PAL, BPF, or pneumothorax with ongoing air leak. Case reports, case series, and observational studies with extractable pediatric data were included. Two reviewers independently screened, assessed eligibility, and abstracted data; findings were synthesized narratively. RESULTS: Thirteen reports were included. Valve placement achieved rapid or eventual air-leak improvement in selected children, including those with necrotizing pneumonia, postoperative air leak, chronic ventilator dependence, malignancy, and ECMO support. Reported complications included valve migration or loosening, granulation tissue, minor hemoptysis, atelectasis, contralateral pneumothorax, and recurrent air leak, although many children underwent valve removal without complication. CONCLUSION: Endobronchial or intrabronchial valve placement may be a useful rescue or bridge therapy for carefully selected children with refractory PAL or BPF. Evidence remains low certainty owing to small samples, retrospective design, inconsistent outcome definitions, and possible publication bias. Prospective multicenter registries with standardized reporting are needed to define optimal selection, timing, and safety.

title: Effects on health and antioxidant status of oral supplementation of hazelnut skin extract in dairy calves with neonatal diarrhea: a randomized clinical trial in hospitalized patients.
authors: Boccardo A, Sannazzaro M, Sala G, Gazzola E, Martucci I, Curone G, Castrica M, Ferrulli V
abstract: Neonatal calf diarrhea (NCD) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in calves. Growing concern about antimicrobial resistance has spurred interest in phytotherapeutic alternatives, particularly polyphenol-rich extracts. Hazelnut skin (HS), a by-product of the confectionery sector, is a sustainable and underutilized source of polyphenols; however, its therapeutic efficacy in calves with NCD remains insufficiently investigated. This randomized, parallel-group clinical trial evaluated the effects of oral HS extract supplementation as an adjunct to standard medical therapy in hospitalized dairy calves with NCD. Sixty female Holstein calves were randomly allocated to a control group (CTRL; n = 30) or a treatment group (HS; n = 30) receiving 10 g/day of HS extract with milk for 5 days. All calves received standardized clinical management, including fluid therapy and antimicrobial administration. Clinical parameters, milk intake, body weight, hospitalization outcomes, sepsis scores, and blood oxidative stress biomarkers were monitored. No significant differences were detected between groups for clinical recovery, fecal score, hydration status, milk intake, weight gain, hospitalization duration, mortality, or oxidative stress markers. Clinical improvement over time was evident in both groups and was attributable to standard therapy. In conclusion, short-term oral supplementation with HS extract did not confer additional clinical or antioxidant benefits when added to conventional treatment in calves with NCD.

title: Acute Kidney Disease and Clinical Outcomes in Stable Outpatients With Decompensated Cirrhosis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
authors: Lekakis V, Wong F, Papatheodoridis G, Vlachogiannakos J, Cholongitas E
journal: Journal of clinical and experimental hepatology
abstract: BACKGROUND/AIMS: Acute kidney disease (AKD), as recently redefined by the Acute Disease Quality Initiative-International Club of Ascites (ADQI-ICA) consensus, captures persistent or subacute kidney dysfunction often following acute kidney injury (AKI). Its prognostic relevance in stable outpatients with decompensated cirrhosis remains insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of AKD and its phenotypes (AKI-AKD and non-AKI AKD [NAKI-AKD]) with cirrhosis-related complications and mortality in outpatients with stable decompensated cirrhosis. METHODS: In this prospective real-world study, 131 patients were followed for up to 60 mo. AKD was defined according to ADQI-ICA criteria and modeled as a time-dependent exposure. Complications were analyzed using Poisson incidence rate and cause-specific Cox models. Mortality was assessed using Aalen-Johansen estimates and time-dependent cause-specific Cox regression, with liver transplantation considered a competing event and parsimonious adjustment for baseline liver disease severity. RESULTS: AKD developed in 51 patients (38.9%). The overall complication-event rate was higher following AKD onset than during AKD-free follow-up (183.3 vs 36.6 per 100 person-years; adjusted incidence rate ratio: 4.91, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.01-8.03; P < 0.001). In the MELD 3.0-adjusted model, the mortality hazard was highest during the AKD period (0-90 d after onset [adjusted cause-specific hazard ratio (aCsHR): 27.07, 95% CI: 11.83-61.90; P < 0.001]) and remained elevated during the late follow-up after AKD (aCsHR: 8.77, 95% CI: 4.00-19.23; P < 0.001). Among patients with AKD, AKI-AKD was associated with higher mortality than NAKI-AKD (aCsHR: 3.07, 95% CI: 1.46-6.47; P = 0.003). CONCLUSION: AKD is common among stable outpatients with decompensated cirrhosis and was associated with a graded risk of complications and death. Phenotypic stratification identifies AKI-AKD as the highest-risk subgroup, although these findings require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice.
authors: Nobile B, Courtet P
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI's potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians' confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scientific rigor.

title: Breaking the degenerative triad: Microenvironment reprogramming biomaterials for intervertebral disc regeneration.
authors: Zhao X, Han X, Hu Z, Chen Y, Wang X, Liu Q, Hu X, Zhang Q
abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) represents a leading cause of chronic low back pain worldwide, imposing considerable public health and socioeconomic burdens. Current clinical interventions remain largely palliative, unable to reverse the progressive pathological cascade. This cascade is driven by a core self-amplifying triad of oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and nutrient deprivation within the unique avascular, high-load disc niche, and ultimately progresses to end-stage terminal phenotypes such as biomechanical failure and neurovascular ingrowth. Over recent years, biomaterial-based regenerative strategies have evolved from passive structural fillers toward multifunctional platforms capable of active microenvironmental reprogramming. This review provides a systematic, critical synthesis of state-of-the-art advances in the field, organized within a hierarchical framework spanning immunometabolic modulation of the degenerative niche and targeted delivery of cellular and molecular therapeutics with further elaboration of precision-stratified design and whole-disc tissue engineering. We critically appraise evidence maturity across different strategy classes and dissect disc-specific translational barriers, noting that most candidate platforms remain at preclinical validation stages. Building on this analysis, we outline priority research directions and realistic near-term translational milestones to guide rational development of next-generation regenerative platforms toward durable functional disc repair.

title: A topologically engineered hydrogel platform targeting IL11 promotes renal repair after partial nephrectomy.
authors: Yu Z, Dong X, Li F, Zhang Y, Dai S, Cao N, Jia X, Zhao J
abstract: Partial nephrectomy (PN) is the gold standard for treating renal tumors and trauma; however, massive nephron loss and persistent fibrosis readily lead to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Current therapeutic options remain non-curative and costly, as nearly half of PN patients inevitably progress to end-stage renal failure. Here, we present an innovative regenerative platform for PN-induced CKD, integrating structural biomimicry with targeted molecular inhibition. Harnessing light-based bioprinting of gelatin and hyaluronic acid methacrylates coupled with removable alginate microfiber, we constructed a hierarchical channel scaffold (HCS) that features precisely patterned macrochannels and template-derived microchannels, which closely mimics native kidney architecture, provides structural support, and remarkably enhances cell migration (∼5.45-fold) and rapid neovascularization (∼7.66-fold) over unidirectional channel structures. Moreover, interleukin 11 (IL11) was identified as a novel therapeutic target in kidney fibrosis after PN. Thus, extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from mesenchymal stem cells loaded with IL11 small interfering RNA (siIL11) were homogeneously encapsulated into HCS, achieving over 4-fold higher renal retention than systemic delivery in PN-induced CKD mice. Furthermore, sustained local release of EV-siIL11 and hierarchically channeled HCS guided synergistic regenerative effects that remarkably inhibited fibrosis, cell cycle arrest, and immune responses, thereby potently preventing kidney atrophy and restoring renal structure with newly aligned nephrons and vasculature, ultimately recovering kidney function. Further analysis revealed that IL11 silencing reversed epithelial‒mesenchymal transition by suppressing the STAT3-ERK-GSK3β-SNAI1 axis. This topological multifunctional hydrogel platform offers a localized, sustained, and clinically translatable strategy for postsurgical kidney regeneration.

title: Postoperative infections after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass - incidence, performance of diagnostic procedures, and predictive factors.
authors: Erixon C, Johannesson E, Dardashti A, Melhammar L, Nilsson J, Thelaus L, Linder A, Zindovic I
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cardiac surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) induces a systemic inflammatory response that affects common inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), white blood cell count (WBC), and body temperature, complicating postoperative diagnosis of infections. The objective of this study was to assess the incidence of postoperative infections and evaluate the performance of clinically used biomarkers. DESIGN: This was a bidirectional cohort study including patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB between 1st of February 2020 and 22nd of September 2021. Patients with postoperative infection were compared to patients without. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of postoperative infections. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves evaluated the diagnostic ability of current biomarkers to detect infection. RESULTS: A total of 1,222 patients were included. The incidence of postoperative infections (during hospitalisation and/or late infection) was 17.3%. Patients with postoperative infection had more comorbidities, underwent more complex procedures, and had higher mortality (90-day mortality 3.8% vs 1.5%, p = 0.045; 1-year mortality 5.7% vs 2.7%, p = 0.032). CRP, WBC, and temperature performed poorly in detecting postoperative infection, although peak CRP (OR 1.069, p < 0.001) and peak temperature (OR 2.408, p = 0.005) were independent predictors of postoperative infection. Peak temperature occurred on postoperative day 5 in infected patients versus day 2 in those without infection. CONCLUSION: Postoperative infections following cardiac surgery with CPB remain common and are associated with increased postoperative complications and mortality. Common inflammatory biomarkers perform poorly in detecting infection. Improved diagnostic tools are needed to facilitate early detection and treatment.

title: Modelling the effect of interventions to prevent MRSA transmission within hospitals in Edmonton, Canada.
authors: Li R, Deardon R, Li N, Conly J, Leal J
abstract: Hospitalized patients are particularly susceptible to infections brought on by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and these infections usually have a high morbidity and mortality rate. Several strategies can help prevent MRSA from spreading, but the efficacy of each strategy remains unclear, as most past research evaluated multiple interventions together rather than examining each one individually. To assess the effects of hand hygiene and screening, we created a novel compartmental MRSA spread framework for healthcare facilities in Edmonton, Alberta. The model accounts for MRSA patients (hospital-acquired (HA) MRSA or community-acquired (CA) MRSA colonization or infections) and isolated patients. To examine the effects of interventions, we first estimated the posterior mean of the parameters in our model, as well as a sub-model of it, using a Bayesian framework with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques, utilizing data from hospitals in Edmonton. Next, we incorporated different intervention rates into the model to ascertain their effect on colonized and infected patients. One intervention is practicing hand hygiene among healthcare workers in hospitals to reduce transmission rates between susceptible individuals and MRSA patients. The other intervention is to screen patients for MRSA colonization to place them in isolation rooms swiftly. The two interventions were first examined alone, and then simultaneously. We compared the overall number of HA-MRSA colonization and infections as the intervention rates varied, and the findings show that combined interventions are more effective than individual interventions at limiting MRSA transmission in hospitals.

title: Hemodynamic effects of ventilating or not, during cardiopulmonary bypass in a porcine model.
authors: Kvalheim VL, Mongstad A, Husby P, Stangeland L, Nginamau ES, Osman TA, Yamada S, Grong K
abstract: Background. Optimal ventilator setting during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is unknown. Improved gas exchange and lung compliance have been suggested as favourable outcomes when lungs are ventilated. However, long-time effects have been hard to demonstrate. There has been less focus on the immediate circulatory effects of ventilator settings during cardioplegia and CPB, and potentially hemodynamic effects of different ventilator strategies are unknown. Methods. Sixteen anesthetized pigs on normothermic CPB with 80 min of aortic cross-clamp and cardioplegic arrest were randomized to a ventilated and a not ventilated group. After weaning, both cardiac-, hemodynamic-, and pulmonary functions were evaluated for up to 120 min. Results. Left ventricular variables and cardiac output did not differ between the two study groups, neither before nor after weaning. After weaning, mean pulmonary artery pressure was increased in ventilated compared to not ventilated animals. Neither pulmonary compliance nor oxygen uptake differed between groups in surviving animals. Conclusions. Disconnection of the ventilator during CPB and cardiac arrest did not affect lung compliance and oxygen uptake, neither positively nor negatively. In the ventilated group, a temporary increase in the pulmonary pressure after weaning was observed.

title: Clinical Outcomes following invasive coronary angiography for patients with acute coronary syndromes pretreated with P2Y12 inhibitors and considered for urgent coronary artery bypass graft surgery.
authors: Lim CJ, Singh M, Sammut MA, Faizur Rahman ME, Parker WAE, Sadeque SAA, Storey RF
abstract: This retrospective single-centre observational study included 262 sequential patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS) undergoing invasive coronary angiography (ICA) while receiving P2Y12 inhibitors and considered for coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG); P2Y12 inhibitors (ticagrelor 91%, thienopyridine 9%) were stopped prior to CABG. The primary outcome was recurrent myocardial infarction or death following ICA and prior to revascularisation or decision for conservative management. 2 patients (0.8%) had recurrent MI and died following ICA and prior to planned CABG, demonstrating a small risk of MI and death in patients who have delays to CABG following ICA for ACS.

title: Circulatory arrest versus aortic cross-clamping in proximal thoracic aortic aneurysm repair.
authors: Braatz E, Stenman M, Al-Mousli J, Dalén M, Olsson C
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Aortic cross‑clamping and mild hypothermic circulatory arrest (MHCA) are commonly used strategies in proximal thoracic aortic aneurysm surgery. This study compared these approaches in elective procedures for patients with a distal ascending aortic diameter of 40-50 mm. The primary outcome was a composite of 30‑day mortality, stroke, or acute kidney injury, with secondary outcomes including long‑term survival and postoperative complications. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This single‑center observational cohort included patients treated between 2016 and 2024. Distal ascending aortic diameters were assessed on preoperative computed tomography, and clinical data were obtained from SWEDEHEART. Patients were assigned to aortic cross‑clamp (n = 261) or MHCA (n = 138). Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 ratio to balance baseline characteristics. RESULTS: The composite primary outcome occurred in 15 patients (3.8%) and was more common with MHCA than with cross‑clamp (6.5% vs 2.3%, p = 0.035). Two patients (0.5%), both in the MHCA group, died within 30 days. After matching, the odds ratio for the composite endpoint was 2.4 (95% CI, 0.66-11.5), indicating no significant difference. Long‑term survival was similar between groups (log‑rank p = 0.33). CONCLUSIONS: Both strategies were associated with low perioperative risk and comparable long‑term survival. These results support flexible operative planning, allowing the distal anastomotic technique to be chosen based on individual anatomy and surgical preference.

title: Gel Immersion Endoscopic Mucosal Resection With Submucosal Injection for Superficial Esophageal Squamous Neoplasms (With Video).
authors: Uda T, Urabe Y, Gurita T, Hatsushika Y, Masuda S, Sako Y, Nakamura T, Kamigaichi Y
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Gel immersion can provide a stable immersion environment during endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). However, its application in superficial esophageal squamous lesions remains limited. In this study, we evaluated a gel immersion EMR (GI-EMR) technique in which submucosal injection was intentionally performed before snaring for selected small superficial esophageal squamous lesions. METHODS: This single-center, retrospective case series included consecutive patients who underwent GI-EMR with submucosal injection for superficial esophageal squamous lesions ≤15 mm in size between January and March 2026. The primary outcome was the histological en bloc resection rate, while secondary outcomes included technical success, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, procedure time, adverse events, and histopathological findings. RESULTS: GI-EMR with submucosal injection was attempted for 13 lesions, achieving a technical success rate of 92% (12/13). One procedure was discontinued because adequate lifting could not be achieved due to post-chemoradiotherapy scarring. The endoscopic and histological en bloc resection rates were both 85% (11/13) on an intention-to-treat basis. The median procedure time was 4.25 min (range, 2.0-11.0 min). No intraoperative or delayed perforation, post-procedure bleeding, or gel-related adverse events occurred. CONCLUSIONS: GI-EMR with submucosal injection was technically feasible for selected superficial esophageal squamous lesions ≤15 mm, with no serious procedure-related adverse events observed in this small case series. TRIAL REGISTRATION: N/A.

title: Physicians' perspectives of palliative care quality in nursing homes: a cross-sectional study.
authors: Sandsdalen T, Hov R, Sanaker H, Ødbehr LS
journal: Scandinavian journal of primary health care
abstract: BACKGROUND: Since physicians have primary responsibility for medical treatment, their perspectives of palliative care quality in nursing homes can provide important knowledge for service evaluation and enhancement in this context. However, few studies exist that include their perspectives. OBJECTIVES: The aim was to investigate physicians' perspectives of the quality of palliative care in Norwegian nursing homes. METHODS: A cross-sectional study conducted between November 2022 and December 2023, which included 77 nursing home physicians (response rate 43.5%) in Norway. Data were collected using a questionnaire comprising questions about demographic variables and perceptions of quality of care, as measured by the short form of the instrument Quality from the Patients' Perspective for Palliative Care (QPP-PC), adapted for healthcare personnel. Descriptive analyses and Wilcoxon signed rank tests were performed. RESULTS: Nursing home physicians scored subjective importance of the care significantly higher than their perception of the quality of actual care received in the two dimensions; medical-technical competence and sociocultural atmosphere and for nine out of the 24 items and three out of seven additional symptom-specific questions. A need for improvement was identified in care areas such as symptom relief for pain, depression and anxiety, existential care, understanding patients' perspective, waiting time, individualized care, cooperation, and continuity. CONCLUSION: The results show that provision of high-quality palliative care in nursing homes can be challenging and that the physicians identified several areas for improvement. The results can provide direction for future quality improvement. However, the findings need to be confirmed in a larger sample.

title: Sex- and age-specific trends in prescription medication use, 2005-2025: a nationwide repeated cross-sectional study.
authors: Roland N, Ernst MT, Linde JJ, Rasmussen L, Pottegård A
abstract: BACKGROUND: Previous studies have documented higher medication consumption among females than males; however contemporary sex-based differences across age and therapeutic classes remain poorly characterized. METHODS: We used the Danish National Prescription Registry to identify all prescriptions redeemed by Danish adults in 2005, 2015 and 2025, assessing overall medication use by sex and age. For the 30 most prescribed therapeutic classes, age-adjusted rate ratios (aRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated to compare use between sexes. Polypharmacy (≥ five medications redeemed within a calendar year) was also assessed by sex and age groups. FINDINGS: In 2025, females accounted for 52% of total medication consumption (1.98 billion Defined Daily Doses (DDDs) among females vs. 3.82 billion DDDs overall), down from 60% (1.17 billion vs. 1.96 billion DDDs) in 2005. This female excess was confined to early adulthood; from age 55 onward, male consumption exceeded that of females. While some of the higher medication use reflected a higher prevalence of certain conditions among females (e.g., thyroid disorders, osteoporosis, depression), females also exhibited a higher use of mental health medications, including antipsychotics, and, newly in 2025, ADHD medications (aRR 1.25; 95%CI 1.16-1.34). Males more frequently used cardiovascular therapies (antithrombotic agents (0.64; 0.62-0.66), insulins (0.67; 0.65-0.69)). However, the historical male cardiovascular predominance was challenged in 2025: thiazide diuretics (1.19; 1.16-1.22) and non-insulin glucose-lowering drugs were more prescribed to females (1.08; 1.01-1.16). Polypharmacy was more common among females in early adulthood but converged after age 65. INTERPRETATION: Sex-based differences in overall medication use have narrowed over time. There is a need for continued monitoring of persistent and emerging sex differences in prescribing. FUNDING: No specific funding.

title: The role of PANSS-G12-rated clinical insight in self-reporting the impact of symptoms in patients with schizophrenia living in the community.
authors: Frigola-Capell E, González-Caballero JL, Cid J, Romero-López-Alberca C, Ochoa S, Vila-Badia R, Salvador-Carulla L, Moreno-Küstnerh B
abstract: BACKGROUND: Impaired insight is common in schizophrenia and may influence the interpretation of patient-reported outcome measures, which are increasingly used in patient-centred care and research. However, little is known about how insight relates to self-reported symptom impact. This study examined this relationship in people with schizophrenia in community settings. METHODS: Latent class analysis was applied to responses from 162 participants on the Patient-Reported Impact of Symptoms in Schizophrenia (PRISS) scale. Sociodemographic, clinical and functional disability variables were analysed as predictors of class membership. Insight was assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) G12 item in a subset of participants. Invariance analyses evaluated the consistency of the latent class structure across samples and gender. RESULTS: A four-class model was identified: Low symptom impact (50.62%); Disorganisation (26.54%); Suspiciousness (10.5%); and Severe (12.35%). The Severe clas showed a higher prevalence of clinician-rated negative symptoms. No association was observed between PANSS-G12-rated clinical insight and self-reported negative symptoms. The latent class structure was invariant across samples and gender, although women more frequently reported disturbance of volition, depression and feelings of guilt. Disability, psychological treatment and hospitalisation history were associated with class membership. CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest that impaired PANSS-G12-rated clinical insight is associated with greater self-reported impact of disorganisation and suspiciousness, but not with the self-reported impact of negative symptoms. Four distinct profiles of symptom impact were identified, with self-reported depression being more prevalent in the most severe profile. These findings may support patient-centred assessment in schizophrenia.

title: Screening a thermotolerant Komagataella phaffii strain with methanol cross-tolerance and the associated physiological and transcriptional responses.
authors: Li C, Jiang T, Bo Y, Lu Z, Zhou Y, Zhang G
abstract: Komagataella phaffii is a prominent methylotrophic yeast widely used in industrial biotechnology for heterologous protein production, chemical synthesis, and C1 feedstock utilization. However, its industrial application is limited by thermal stress and methanol toxicity, while the relationship between heat adaptation and methanol tolerance remains poorly understood. Here, we obtained a thermotolerant mutant ATH through ARTP mutagenesis followed by adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) under heat stress (37 °C). ATH tolerated heat and methanol robustly under individual stress conditions, achieving 3-fold and 8-fold higher cell densities than GS115 at 37 °C or in 5% (v/v) methanol, respectively, yet failed under the combined stress of 37 °C and 5% methanol. Using three proteins (GFP, OPH, and ChiA) as reporters, we found that ATH showed higher heterologous expression than GS115 at 33 °C. Physiologically, ATH displayed enhanced cell wall/membrane integrity, reduced ROS accumulation and lower lipid peroxidation (>30% reduction in MDA), and accelerated formaldehyde clearance. Transcriptomics identified 561 shared differentially expressed genes, with coordinated upregulation of heat shock proteins (HSP70/40/90 families; Hsp104 and Hsp70-SSA2), antioxidant enzymes (catalase, peroxiredoxin), and cell wall/membrane remodeling genes, alongside downregulation of amino acid and secondary metabolite biosynthesis. Whole-genome resequencing further distinguished ATH from GS115 by only 19 variants (9 SNPs and 10 InDels), highlighting a compact genetic basis for the evolved phenotype. This work provides a K. phaffii chassis with improved individual heat and methanol tolerance and elucidates the physiological, transcriptional, and genomic mechanism underlying heat-methanol cross-adaptation.

title: Cold-induced transcriptomic responses are associated with strain-dependent Salmonella enterica persistence in refrigerated lettuce leaves.
authors: Rodríguez-Alvarez Y, González N, Araya MP, Moreno-Switt AI, Melotto M, Jacob C
abstract: Salmonella enterica is a leading cause of foodborne outbreaks linked to leafy greens. Refrigerated storage is a cornerstone of leafy-green safety, yet strain-level variation in the persistence of internalized S. enterica under these conditions remains poorly understood. Screening of eleven S. enterica strains revealed marked differences in their persistence within detached romaine lettuce leaves stored at 10 °C. Two isolates, belonging to serovars Montevideo and Newport, displaying contrasting persistence phenotypes were selected for detailed analysis, and these differences were confirmed at 4 °C. To investigate transcriptional responses associated with this variation, we profiled transcriptomic responses to cold stress in nutrient-rich medium by RNA-seq and evaluated post-cold recovery. Both isolates grew similarly at 28 °C but diverged at 4 °C, with the Montevideo strain maintaining higher growth capacity. Functional enrichment of KEGG pathways and Gene Ontology terms revealed shared repression of central metabolic and energy-producing pathways, coupled with induction of stress-response processes. Genes associated with general stress responses, cold-shock functions, and envelope integrity were more prominently represented among the induced responses of the Montevideo strain after cold exposure. These findings indicate that strain-dependent differences in Salmonella persistence during refrigerated lettuce storage are associated with distinct transcriptional responses to cold stress and post-cold recovery phenotypes observed in cultured bacteria. Consideration of strain-level variation may improve interpretation of pathogen persistence during leafy-green storage and inform future microbial risk assessments.

title: Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) Mapping and Visualization of Pre-Implementation Determinants for Sepsis Care Transitions.
authors: You SB, Stawnychy MA, Song J, Hirschman KB, O'Connor M, Sang E, Oh S, Pitcher K
abstract: INTRODUCTION: High-quality care transitions are essential for sepsis survivors at risk of readmission and long-term complications. These complex innovations require coordination across organizations, individuals, and processes. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) offers a systematic approach to identifying multi-level implementation determinants, but translating them into actionable strategies remains challenging. This study examines the representation of implementation determinants across CFIR domains and visualizes their cross-domain interconnectedness. METHODS: CFIR-guided, semi-structured pre-implementation needs assessment interviews were conducted with stakeholders involved in sepsis care transitions across five hospital-home healthcare (HHC) dyads. Thirty-two themes identified through deductive-inductive coding were mapped to CFIR domains and constructs and visualized using node diagrams. RESULTS: Sixty-one interviews with 91 stakeholders identified 32 themes spanning all five CFIR domains, with most themes mapping to multiple domains. Access to Care theme mapped across all five domains, while External Policies and Incentives and Informal Caregiving themes were represented only once. Implementation Process domain was most represented and Innovation least represented. All constructs within the Implementation Process and Individual Characteristics domains were captured. Node diagrams illustrated the depth and interconnected influence of determinants in sepsis care transitions. CONCLUSIONS: Stakeholders identified complexity emerged across technical, structural, and policy domains as both an innovation feature and contextual determinants of sepsis care transitions. CFIR mapping and visualization provided a structured approach to characterizing pre-implementation complexity in sepsis care transitions. Examining determinant representation and cross-domain interconnectedness may help identify cross-cutting, potentially high-leverage implementation needs and inform strategy selection and tailoring for complex hospital-to-home interventions.

title: Identification of Tex and the Phage Shock Protein YthA as putative FtsH substrates associated with the cell envelope stress response in Lactococcus cremoris.
authors: Rendueles C, Escobedo S, Campelo AB, Alonso-Fernández S, Rau MH, Gaspar P, Narberhaus F, Martínez B
abstract: As part of the Cell Envelope Stress (CES) response orchestrated by the two-component system CesSR in lactococci, the FtsH protease is expected to play a role in counteracting stress, as observed in other bacteria. However, neither its specific role nor its substrates have been identified in this genus. The primary objective of this study was therefore to elucidate the FtsH function in the context of CES. A Lactococcus cremoris NZ9000 ΔftsH exhibited an extended lag phase, increased salt and heat sensitivity and lysozyme resistance. However, only the salt and heat sensitive phenotype could be restored by complementation of the ftsH deletion. Whole-genome sequencing revealed putative compensatory mutations in ΔftsH, including genes encoding a transcriptional regulator and components of ABC transporters. Although awaiting experimental validation, these mutations may nevertheless underscore the broader physiological significance of FtsH in L. cremoris. Furthermore, a comparative proteomic analysis of L. cremoris NZ9000 ΔftsH under CES conditions identified putative FtsH substrates. In vivo degradation experiments demonstrated an extended half-life of the RNA-binding protein Tex and the Phage-Shock Protein YthA in a growth-phase dependent manner, thereby proposing these proteins as putative FtsH substrates in L. cremoris. While the specific function of Tex remains to be elucidated, the regulated degradation of YthA suggests that proteolysis may represent an additional regulatory layer within the lactococcal CES response.

title: Aversive learning retroactively modulates neutral episodic memories structured by prior knowledge of predictive sequences.
authors: Baczkowski BM, Villringer A
abstract: Linking memories of temporally separated neutral and threatening experiences can support later recognition of early warning signals. Yet it remains unclear what cognitive processes might allow the seemingly inconsequential neutral events - encoded in safe contexts and thus prone to forgetting - to nevertheless be preserved in memory well enough to inform future threat predictions. Here, we tested whether Pavlovian threat conditioning retroactively strengthens long-term episodic memory for previously encoded neutral events by leveraging prior knowledge of their predictive relations. Young adults first learned to anticipate the order of semantic categories in two deterministic sequences (A → B → C and D → E → F) through repeated presentation of images depicting category exemplars. They then incidentally encoded trial-unique exemplars from each category during sequence viewing. In a next phase, exemplars from the third-position categories were repeated such that one (C) predicted mild electric shocks, whereas the other (F) was never reinforced, creating a category-level threat association through conditioning. After 24 h, recognition memory for exemplars of categories encoded before conditioning depended on sequence and position: when a sequence ended with a shock-predictive category, memory favored the starting category (A) over the following category (B) - an effect absent in the control categories (D and E). These results suggest that aversive learning can retroactively reshape episodic memories of neutral events when they are scaffolded by prior sequence knowledge, bridging temporal gaps and thereby potentially promoting early threat anticipation.

title: Seasonal dynamic model for projecting tuberculosis epidemiological trends in Kyrgyzstan.
authors: Altynai B, Lou P, Gulmira K, Shauer D, Xu J, Wang K
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health burden in Kyrgyzstan; however, the seasonal transmission dynamics of TB in the country have not been quantitatively characterized. This study aimed to develop a seasonal dynamic model to simulate TB transmission, estimate the basic reproduction number R 0, assess transmission intensity, and inform evidence-based prevention and control strategies. Using monthly reported new TB cases from the national TB surveillance and registration system in Kyrgyzstan from 2022 to 2025, we constructed a seasonal SEIR model incorporating periodic transmission and reactivation rates. Model parameters were estimated using a Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. R 0 was calculated using two methods: the periodic time-varying method and the annual average transmission rate method. Local sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the impact of the baseline transmission parameter a s and the baseline reactivation parameter a e on TB transmission dynamics. The model adequately captured the seasonal fluctuations and overall downward trend in new TB cases, achieving a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.66% and a root mean square percentage error (RMSPE) of 9.95%. The estimated periodic R 0 was 0.8842 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 0.8811-0.8873), which remained below the threshold of unity. Assuming no change in current prevention and control measures, projections suggest a gradual decline in monthly new TB cases, with the annual number of new cases declining to approximately 2902 by 2126. These results indicate that TB transmission has not been fully interrupted and that elimination is unlikely to be achieved within the projection period. Sensitivity analysis revealed that both a s and a e substantially affected the number of new TB cases and R 0, and that modest changes in these parameters could drive R 0 above the threshold of unity. The seasonal SEIR model provided a good fit to the monthly number of new TB cases in Kyrgyzstan. Although the estimated R 0 is below the threshold of unity, indicating a declining epidemic trend, the rate of decline remains relatively slow, highlighting the need to sustain and strengthen prevention and control measures.

title: From laboratory quantification to rapid on-site testing: Screening of high-affinity monoclonal antibody pairs targeting the RSV F protein and analytical evaluation across multiple assay platforms.
authors: Peng S, Liu Q, Duan C, Liu J, Wang R, Huang Y, Long A, Deng Q
abstract: Monoclonal antibodies against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) F protein are key reagents for antigen-based diagnosis, yet antibody pairs compatible with multiple assay formats remain limited. In this study, BALB/c mice were immunized with recombinant postfusion RSV F protein, yielding six hybridoma cell lines secreting anti-RSV F monoclonal antibodies. The antibodies were characterized by indirect ELISA, Western blotting, and surface plasmon resonance, and the optimal sandwich pair was selected by cross-pairing ELISA. The mAb-14/mAb-26 pair showed high affinity and the best pairing performance and was used to establish double-antibody sandwich ELISA (DAS-ELISA), magnetic microparticle-based chemiluminescent immunoassay, and Au@Pt nanoparticle-based lateral flow immunoassay (Au@Pt-LFIA). The limits of detection were 0.25, 0.04, and 0.78 ng/mL, respectively. Au@Pt-LFIA achieved an approximately fourfold lower visual detection limit than conventional colloidal gold immunochromatography without additional signal-amplification steps. None of the three methods showed detectable cross-reactivity with the seven tested heterologous respiratory pathogen antigens. In preliminary clinical sample testing, the positive percent agreements of DAS-ELISA, chemiluminescent immunoassay, and Au@Pt-LFIA were 90.0%, 93.3%, and 83.3%, respectively, and the negative percent agreements were 100.0% for all methods. These results support mAb-14/mAb-26 as a versatile antibody pair for RSV antigen detection across complementary laboratory and on-site assay platforms.

title: Environmental Impact of Conventional Versus Underwater Endoscopic Mucosal Resection for Colorectal Lesions: A Procedure-Based Life Cycle Assessment With Pooled Effectiveness Estimates.
authors: Calabrese G, Moll F, Neves JAC, Bonacci L, Sinagra E, Castiglione F, Maida M, Albéniz-Arbizu E
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The environmental impact of endoscopic techniques remains poorly defined. We compared procedure-related environmental outcomes between conventional endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) and underwater EMR (U-EMR) for colorectal lesions. METHODS: In this prospective pilot procedure-based life cycle assessment of the resection phase, 10-25-mm colorectal lesions underwent EMR or U-EMR across three endoscopy units. Outcomes included global warming potential (GWP, kg CO2-equivalent/procedure), waste, life-cycle water consumption, fossil resource scarcity, and terrestrial acidification. Exploratory GWP per en bloc resection was estimated using pooled randomized-trial and pilot-cohort data. RESULTS: Forty-nine procedures were included: 23 EMR and 26 U-EMR. En bloc resection was achieved in 56.5% of EMR and 69.2% of U-EMR, and R0 resection in 52.2% and 69.2%. Mean GWP was significantly lower with U-EMR than EMR (1.92 ± 0.54 vs. 2.42 ± 0.50 kg CO2-eq; p = 0.002), corresponding to a reduction of 0.50 kg CO2-eq per procedure and 50 kg CO2-eq per 100 procedures. U-EMR was associated with lower waste generation (324.0 ± 78.3 vs. 407.3 ± 72.0 g; p < 0.001), water consumption (0.56 ± 0.17 vs. 0.77 ± 0.20 m3; p < 0.001), fossil resource scarcity (0.33 ± 0.10 vs. 0.40 ± 0.09 kg oil-eq; p = 0.007), and terrestrial acidification (0.0052 ± 0.0018 vs. 0.0068 ± 0.0018 kg SO2-eq; p = 0.003). Findings were consistent across scenario and uncertainty analyses. In the meta-analysis-based model, GWP per en bloc resection was lower with U-EMR than EMR (2.59 vs. 3.51 kg CO2-eq), corresponding to a 26.3% relative reduction. CONCLUSIONS: U-EMR was associated with lower procedure-related environmental burden than conventional EMR, persisting after normalization for en bloc resection. TRIAL REGISTRATION: No. 165/26.

title: Feasibility of a Deep-Learning Model for Objective Visualization-Quality Assessment During Cholangioscopy-Guided Lithotripsy: A Proof-of-Concept Study.
authors: Kamada H, Kobayashi K, Yamana H, Fujita N, Namima D, Yamada M, Fujita S, Suto H
abstract: During peroral cholangioscopy-guided electrohydraulic lithotripsy (EHL), stone fragmentation obscures the visual field (the "snowstorm effect"), and visualization quality has been assessed only subjectively. This proof-of-concept study explored the feasibility of a deep-learning method for objectively quantifying visualization quality during EHL and, as an exploratory application, compared viscous gel immersion with saline irrigation. A ResNet-18 model was trained on expert-annotated frames (5-point scale) from three development cases. For independent validation, 120 frames from 12 previously unseen comparison cases were scored by two blinded endoscopists (inter-reader weighted κ = 0.98). The model showed only moderate agreement with their consensus (weighted κ = 0.60; accuracy 70.8%); because the validation sample was enriched for predicted-usable frames, metrics re-weighted to the natural frame distribution gave sensitivity 29.8% and specificity 93.5%, indicating systematic under-detection of usable views. Agreement did not differ systematically between gel and saline frames. The High-Quality View Rate (HQVR) was the proportion of EHL-phase frames scored Good/Excellent. In a patient-level comparison, median HQVR was 22.7% for gel versus 8.4% for saline (exact Mann-Whitney U, p = 0.15, not significant); in post hoc exploratory analyses, a threshold-independent mean predicted score differed (1.65 vs. 1.35, p = 0.005) and the longest continuous usable interval favored gel (median 24.4 vs. 5.2 s). Mild cholangitis occurred in 1/5 gel and 4/7 saline patients. Training such a model is feasible, but it is not yet a validated measurement tool, and the gel-versus-saline signal is hypothesis-generating only. Larger multi-case training and prospective validation are required. Trial Registration: N/A.
